(At one point, the chords below the sprightly violins of the track “Spring 1” even contour through the same circular four-note figure that is in the opening of “On the Nature of Daylight.”)

“I had fallen in love with Vivaldi as a tiny kid, but grew to hate it as an adult because you hear it in insurance adverts or when you’re on hold, or whatever. So I wanted to get that out of my system,” Richter said. “I assumed I was going to be destroyed for it—the end of my career. But it’s not like I really had a career.” The record topped classical charts in twenty-two countries. Two years later, Richter came out with a follow-up, a spoken-word album, his mellow voice explaining each piece on the record, DVD-extra style. (Track 9: “ ‘Autumn 1’ is pretty much the original Vivaldi for quite a long time, except I’ve sort of sliced it up and cut holes in it.”) Then, in 2022, he released “The New Four Seasons: Vivaldi Recomposed,” which is the same music, this time made with era-accurate strings, plus one of many Moog synthesizers he owns. “I heard a performance on period instruments and just thought, This is brilliant,” he said. “I thought it was a nice learning journey. A three-hundred-and-sixty-degree project.” His label extended the journey three years later, with “Vivaldi by Max Richter,” which includes tracks from both versions of “Recomposed.” Perhaps a person might save some time by simply listening to Vivaldi.

The masses swooned over the project, but it irritated many musicians. “The way ‘The Four Seasons’ was adopted by the Pottery Barn Muzak crowd already harmed Vivaldi’s status as a serious composer,” Ethan Iverson, a critic and composer, told me. Richter’s own “defanging,” he said, “suggests a future where nobody knows anything about anything: we are all senseless drones, oblivious to the mystery and magic of tonal harmony.”

Not long ago, an A.I. company approached Richter about a potential collaboration. “Their pitch to me was ‘Hey, Max, say you’re writing a song and you get stuck. You’ve got the beginning and you’ve got the end. That’s where we come in. You click this and it’ll fix that for you.’ But that bit is what I live for. That’s where I learn stuff.” He has advocated before British Parliament on the need to protect artists and regulate A.I. Has that been successful? “No, in short.”

Richter believably insists that the art must always come first. “As far as I know, I’m the biggest seller on D.G., but I see that as kind of their problem, not mine,” he said. “I’m very hazy on the commercial side. I don’t love sitting in meetings. The only thing I can control is where I put the notes on the page.”

Richter was born in 1966, in Hamelin, Germany. “It’s where the Pied Piper came from—that’s the only reason anyone knows it,” he said. When he was three, his family moved to Bedford, England, after his father, an electrical engineer, was posted there. His mother, who eventually ran a health-food shop, was an amateur pianist. At age five, Richter started piano lessons: “My teacher was a very lovely elderly woman named Mrs. Hart. If you played a wrong note, she’d hit you with a ruler.”

During Richter’s childhood, the classical world was in the midst of a counterstrike against modernist complexity, which had become an academic norm. In the nineteen-twenties, Arnold Schoenberg had pioneered the twelve-tone method, rejecting the idea of a central key. After the Second World War, this musical language, which yielded a lot of atonal work, became more widely accepted and was further developed by figures like the French serialist composer Pierre Boulez. Artists began to push back against what Richter described as a “modernist hangover,” stripping away the elaborate status quo. In 1964, the composer Terry Riley put out the groundbreaking piece “In C,” which consists of a high C being pinged to eternity for forty minutes, against pulsing instrumentation. Riley’s friend, the New York City-born composer Steve Reich, had suggested the idea of an eighth-note heartbeat—one of many stamps Reich left on the contemporary scene, including “Clapping Music.” Philip Glass, who had studied at Juilliard before doing a Fulbright with the composer Nadia Boulanger, knew Reich and was paring back his own compositions. He soon established the Philip Glass Ensemble for experimental work.

When Richter was twelve, his family milkman offered a portal into this burgeoning new world called minimalism. “He’d be hearing me doing my Mozart, and he took me on as kind of a project,” Richter said. “For me at that time, new music was Stravinsky. But the milkman was a jazz musician, and he had gone to New York and picked up Chatham Square Phillip Glass records and Terry Riley. And he would just drop them off with the milk in the mornings. I was hearing it, going, ‘What is this even?’ ” It became an unquenchable fascination. Richter began, in his words, “scribbling.”

In secondary school, music continued to be a vehicle for his curiosity. “It was an insurgency against a very normalizing, conforming over-all project in the Margaret Thatcher–Ronald Reagan era,” he said. “Really, all I wanted to do was sit around in cafés reading French novels and smoking cigarettes. I stopped going to classes, and they kicked me out.” After completing his A-levels at a training college that had a robust music program, he enrolled at the University of Edinburgh, then transferred to the Royal Academy of Music to study composition. At RAM, modernism was still going strong. “If you were writing tonal music, it just meant that you were an idiot,” he said. They wanted him to write “post-Boulez,” Richter said. “I did that for a while. I wrote very complicated pieces.” But he was drawn back to the intelligibility of minimalism. “The real world makes no sense at all, but a piece of music is a place where things can make sense,” Richter said. “It’s a way of talking about things. And, therefore, I just took everything away. Simplify, simplify, simplify.”

After RAM, Richter moved to Florence to study with Luciano Berio, a pupil of Boulez’s Darmstadt School who later also taught Reich. “Although he was very much a modernist figurehead, Berio was into folk music, historical materials, working with history rather than trying to erase it,” Richter said. “His music was really omnivorous.” (Some people I talked to were surprised that Richter was Berio’s student, but the signs are there: Berio’s “Sinfonia” repurposes Mahler’s Symphony No. 2, serving as an inspiration for Richter’s Vivaldi project.) While working with Berio, Richter engaged with new ideas coming out of the Baltics. “I had heard the very beginning of Arvo Pärt happening,” he said, of the Estonian composer. Pärt developed “tintinnabuli,” a style of two-voice minimalist composition. “I went to his concerts and I said, ‘Hang on, this is amazing.’ So there was lots of stuff that punctured that sort of modernist brain.”

Richter’s style is, no doubt, descended from Pärt. But, in considering Richter’s path, a closer parallel might be Glass—a composer who, despite the judgment of some people in the classical world, made the journey from post-modernist enfant terrible to well-known creator of scores for blockbuster movies (he has been nominated for three Academy Awards, including for “The Hours”). Nico Muhly, a composer who worked closely with Glass, told me that, decades ago, “if you mentioned Philip Glass’s name in academia, it was, like, horses whinny, thunderclaps, lightning strikes. It was some Wicked Witch of the West shit. Nobody was in dialogue with that music. People were actively hostile.” Glass’s crossover into the mainstream, although reviled by certain purists, was momentous. William Robin, the musicologist, said, “When Glass began writing scores, in the eighties, it set a new kind of standard for film, TV, and commercials to have music that is very generic and also emotionally powerful. Richter is doing a similar thing.” On top of the umpteen uses of “Daylight,” Richter has scored countless pieces of media, including “The Leftovers,” “The Veil,” “Spaceman,” and “Ad Astra.” His professional success would not exist without the efforts of Glass.

But Glass, Reich, and Pärt tend to ask more of listeners than Richter does. Their work feels easier to actively engage with, rather than passively absorb. They employ microevolutions—changes of rhythm or placement that make it harder to predict what the ear will catch, despite the cyclicality. As Glass explained in his memoir, “It never repeated all the time, for if it had, it would have been unlistenable.” Richter’s work is not unlistenable. On the contrary: it’s so listenable that you can sometimes forget to listen. When he does make subtle changes—and he does—the impact isn’t as evident. Take “Daylight.” The violin’s floating seesaw melody switches up its suspensions, sometimes holding a note over a measure and sometimes playing it on the downbeat. But it’s loyal to the same type of disruption, and the ear comes to expect it as if it were the norm all along. Perhaps that’s part of his point in the quest to be intelligible, and there are certainly other undercurrent changes that the listener won’t register. But that ultimately means they’re missable.

“If you listen to Max, there are some pieces where there’s a really explicit Glass influence,” Muhly said. “You see that in ‘Vladimir’s Blues,’ ”—a track off of “Blue Notebooks.” He continued, “But, to me, its relationship to Glass is cosmetic,” not structural.

Richter isn’t shy about Glass’s influence, but he skirted the suggestion that his work is derivative of him. “The thing that Glass’s music did for me is it gave permission,” he said. “He brings repetition into the foreground as a somatic idea.” He added, “All music is, in a way, about other music. But repetition is in everything. You know, Chopin’s studies are minimal.” Richter doesn’t have a relationship with Glass (“Our paths have never crossed”), but he’s open to meeting: “Why not? I’m sure he’s a fascinating guy.”

The influence of Richter’s minimalist forebears aside, his project falls more in the comfortable pocket of pop music. (He is planning a show at the Sphere, in Las Vegas, with Oprah Winfrey.) He serves as a gateway for non-musicians to safely enter the classical space. One young composer who has worked with Richter told me, “I used to feel very hostile toward his music. I remember playing this three-hour show, and I was, like, People are sitting through three hours of the same chord progression developing over every minute, going up a fifth every five minutes? This is exhausting for me, and I can’t imagine sitting in the audience listening to it. But people were weeping.” She added, “The market is the market. Maybe there’s something we can learn from that.”

In early September, I visited Richter’s studio, behind an automatic gate in a thirty-one-acre spread near the village of Charlbury, in England. A light rain—rare, after the summer’s heat wave—misted the triangular structure, dappling a glass wall decaled with the letters “SRM”: Studio Richter Mahr. “A big part of this building is about creative community, so we’ve embedded that in the architecture,” Richter explained, standing by an open kitchen in a clinically white foyer. “We’ve got the café in the center, which was very deliberate because it’s a shared space.” Every sound seemed to both echo and disappear instantly. An aide named Joe, who introduced himself as “Mr. Assistant,” brought Richter a small cup of black coffee. (The espresso machine is a La Marzocco Linea PB, which costs as much as a car. Richter said, “I remember in that meeting with the architects, they thought I was joking when I walked in with a brochure for this thing.”)

Richter wore a white shirt rather than his usual black, because, he said, “I’m a bit sleepy this morning.” He’d accessorized with a “Peanuts” watch. “Schroeder’s my guy. He’ll just have a bar of Beethoven in a speech bubble,” he said. “He’s such a pianist.” He led me past a few analog recording machines into the control room—a production area with knobs and screens, and a window onto an open studio. “This room is the end point of the workflow. The whole building is conceived as a kind of an instrument,” he said. “It’s a Henry Ford thing, we’ve got the means of production.” He walked into the recording room. “Oak,” he said, of the walls. “This all comes from a forest in Germany, which has been managed by the same family for two hundred years.” A Steinway D automatic Spirio sat in one corner. A Hammond M102 organ was against the opposite wall. “It’s the same kind of Hammond that Billy Preston played on ‘Abbey Road,’ ” he said. “When I watched that eight-hour documentary, I was just, like, ‘That’s it. I’ve got to have it.’ ” He pointed out the serial number, which dated it to 1967. “The one he plays was lost, and no one knows where it is,” he said, dropping his voice low. “So this could be the one.”

The studio is where Richter created his new album, “While The Flood Rages.” Revision: the music is not exactly new—it’s drawn from his score for a 2022 ballet, “MADDADDAM,” based on a series of post-apocalyptic books by Margaret Atwood. The ballet translates the tale of the rebirth of society after a horrific disaster into egg-forward visuals: egg-headed figures, a giant egg displaying black-and-white footage of industrial cityscapes, interpretive dancing in egg-shaped costumes.

Richter and the director Wayne McGregor began collaborating on “MADDADDAM” in 2019. “The record is not the ballet,” Richter said. “I made some architectural decisions.” He uses his reliable muses—strings, morose bass lines—to represent the harmonious characters known as the Children of Crake. “They’re sort of these synthetic creatures. Genetically, they’re manufactured in a lab,” he explained. “They inherit the Earth from humanity, but that’s a good thing because they’re nonviolent.” The theme closes out each third of the record, including the first single, “Now We Can Sing”—a Pachelbel’s Canon-esque chord cycle, topped by a falling B-major melody that feels a bit like an ear-training interval exercise. It is, in Richter’s words, “existentially safe,” as opposed to a jittering, electronic track called “Data Ballistics,” which sounds, refreshingly, like it could be played at a techno club. To coincide with the album, he released a limited-edition book of crosswords: “1. Broadcast from Howard Stern, e.g.”; “8. Mountain range on the Europe/Asia border.”

Richter introduced me to his wife, the visual artist Yulia Mahr. Her workspace was as white as the foyer. “These guys are tempestuous,” Mahr said, gesturing to a line of ceramic arm sculptures she had made, marbled with dirt and dried weeds, lying on the floor. “They won’t do what they’re asked to do.” Petite and sparkly-eyed, she and Richter first met at the Edinburgh Festival, in the late eighties. “We’ve always just talked ideas,” Richter said. Their partnership brims with creative support—she wears his custom-made Comme des Garçons perfume, which sells for a hundred and sixty-five dollars a bottle and is called “Max Richter 01.” (“We used all the source materials that I work with,” Richter said. “Piano-soundboard wood, rosin, magnetic tape, the insides of synthesizers, the forest.”) Mahr helped come up with the idea for his 2015 album “Sleep,” which was the first classical album to exceed two billion streams across all platforms. It stayed on the Billboard Classical chart for three hundred and fifty-nine weeks. It’s no mystery why: “Sleep” is an eight-and-a-half-hour, two-hundred-and-four-track concept album that you put on before you go to bed. Richter worked with the neuroscientist David Eagleman to learn about the brain during rest, and the record is an ambient—sorry, post-classical—cloud of cyclicality. Richter has described it, as he does “Blue Notebooks,” as “protest music.”

Others might wonder if it’s a gimmick, a ploy to increase streaming numbers masquerading as art. (It does bring to mind Justin Bieber’s desperate attempt to put his song “Yummy” at the top of the charts, in 2020, by urging fans to “create a playlist with ‘Yummy’ on repeat” and “let it play while you sleep.” The song reached No. 2.)

Richter once described “Sleep” as music for when “your conscious mind is on holiday.” He has performed the work live twenty-eight times—the lights are dim, the audience are in beds instead of seats, and the musicians take staggered breaks. Ben Russell, a violinist who often performs with Richter, told me, “You have to really time things and keep your mind interested, otherwise you start to drift. I’ve definitely had some very slow blinks happen during that concert.” Backstage, Richter provides cots and snacks. “You grab a little sushi,” Russell said. “There’s coffee, and even wine helps if you use it judiciously. So sushi, coffee, wine, sushi, coffee, wine.”

One night, I decided to sleep to “Sleep.” I settled into bed around 11 P.M., queued up the first track, and was greeted by pulsing chords on soft keys. I was playing it from my phone, which I imagine most people do, so the low values in each track got lost in the mix, and I found myself being kept alert by the high-end sounds—violins, or a soprano. My conscious mind was not on holiday.

Maybe I would have had a better time napping to the hour-long “From Sleep” (2015), or the slightly longer “Sleep (Remixes)” (2016), or the thirty-minute, electronic-forward “Sleep: Tranquility Base” (2023). Or perhaps I should try a whole night again with “Sleep (Faded)” (2018), which is the same eight and a half hours of music, but with each track fading out at the end. I’ll think it over more, once I finish watching the 2021 documentary “Max Richter’s Sleep,” about Max Richter’s “Sleep.”

Deep in the S.R.M. property, past a large crow-inspired art work by Mahr, there is a secluded patch of trees. “All right, my dears, settle down!” Richter called, by a fence. The dears were his three alpacas—“Paddington, Finn, and . . . I’ve forgotten his name”—who were trying to kick one another in the head. “They’ve gotten frisky with the rain,” he said, beaming. “The dynamics change constantly. It’s the three-alpaca problem.”

The drizzle pattered on his umbrella. “I come out here every day,” he said. “I really enjoy the effect on your thinking, being in the green.” He walked past a row of short dog hurdles set out for his Labrador, Haku, named after a character from “Spirited Away.” “If I’m working on something, I’m here,” he said. “I’ve written movies in hotel rooms, but it’s a pretty torrid experience.” In fact, he wrote a third of the score to “Hamnet” in one.

The project didn’t originally include “On the Nature of Daylight.” “I wrote a different cue for the ending of ‘Hamnet,’ ” he said. “But ‘On the Nature of Daylight’ really got under the skin of the film.” He sounded defeated. “They played it on set, for hours and hours and hours.” The director and co-writer, Chloé Zhao, hadn’t yet finalized the end of the movie, and Jessie Buckley, who starred as Agnes, Hamnet’s mother, sent her “Daylight.” When Zhao listened to it, she had an epiphany about how to wrap up the story—the hands of the audience reaching onto the stage at the Globe Theatre, set to the strains of the twenty-year-old song.

“We had a lot of conversations where I was saying, ‘Look, it’s been in loads of films. I think we need an original score,’ ” Richter said. “It was quite an intense back-and-forth.” (Zhao told IndieWire, in 2025, “We live in a culture that is so afraid not to generate new things.”) Richter went on, “But, ultimately, it’s the director’s baby. Even though I’d written some other music which I personally prefer.”

That piece, called “Of the undiscovered country,” wound up being shovelled to the film’s end credits. I overlaid the final scene with the song, and found myself undistracted by familiarity. As Agnes mourned her son and forgave her husband, the music—high, pearly voices; deep, sombre strings—became a buttress rather than an engine. It allowed the scene to be.

Richter told me that he turns down licensing offers for “Daylight” all the time now, and doesn’t know if he wants it to appear anywhere in the future. “It’s problematic,” he said. “I’m cautious about it because I think it hijacks a movie.” Part of the issue is that British licensing laws allow national TV broadcasts to use the piece without his permission. “So, to some extent, you can’t control it,” he said. He quickly added, “But I’m very grateful.” With thirty-one acres, three alpacas, and a perfume, how could he not be?

One evening, I travelled to Newark, New Jersey, in a downpour to see Richter perform on tour. The PATH train was dotted with flight attendants and World Cup fans. Despite the weather, the New Jersey Performing Arts Center was packed, and Richter’s mass appeal was on full display. A guy downing a Miller Lite sat near a woman in an evening gown. “I listen to him a lot when I read,” a young woman with glasses and a slicked-back ponytail said. This was her first time seeing his music live.

Since Richter emerged as a commercial success, services like Spotify have been flooded with imitators, compiled on such playlists as “Peaceful Strings” (five thousand saves), “Focus Piano” (four hundred thousand saves), and “Peaceful Piano” (nearly eight million saves). In the streaming era, how we consume music has become less intentional—we’re fed what the machine thinks we’ll like, and then more of it. Richter is a cross-genre artist who could lead a listener into the world of classical music, which, in an ever-struggling industry, is a phenomenal contribution. But chances are that an algorithm will feed Richter fans the music of Hans Zimmer or Ludovico Einaudi, and not Dvořák or Messiaen or Fauré. The gateway becomes less of a gateway than an echo chamber.

Blue stage lights dimmed, and Richter, in chunky black glasses and a black shirt, walked out with his ensemble. A rectangular spotlight appeared center stage, like sun coming in from the small window of a stone church. The ensemble began playing “In a Landscape.” Fog-machine smoke billowed across the stage, choreography to the looping bass line.

After intermission, it was finally time for “On the Nature of Daylight.” Slow string notes blossomed out, and the fog wafted into the audience. A couple in front of me huddled closer together. Maybe it was the rain. Maybe I was thinking about dead little Hamnet. Maybe it was because, three nights earlier, my boyfriend had said he wasn’t in love with me. Somewhat against my will, I started to cry. After the piece ended, several people headed toward the exits—they had gotten what they came for. ♦

articles.title: “Grand Theft Auto VI” may mark the end of an era in gaming
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
IT IS NIGHT-TIME in Vice City, Leonida, a raucous digital replica of Miami, Florida. Jason and Lucia, two small-time crooks, have an inauspicious first encounter: they meet while trying to steal the same car. The relationship has a rocky start—Lucia introduces herself to Jason with a baseball bat—but soon the pair are on the run together in the stolen vehicle: partners in life and partners in crime.

So begins the most eagerly awaited video game in history, which launched on November 19th after 13 years of rumours, leaks and missed deadlines. Some analysts predict that “Grand Theft Auto VI” (“GTA VI”) will take more than $3bn worldwide in its first week. That would make it not just the highest-grossing game launch in history, but the biggest entertainment debut of any kind (overtaking “Avengers: Endgame”, a Marvel superhero movie which, by most measures, has held the title since 2019).

Players who had stayed up until midnight to play the game said it was worth the wait. (Some had registered accounts in New Zealand in order to get access a few hours earlier.) “GTA VI” combines the action and irreverent humour of previous titles in the series with an improbably touching love story, played out in an astonishingly lifelike world. On its release, it was the joint-highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, a review aggregator. Employers expect an epidemic of “GTA flu”, as workers call in sick to stay at home playing it.

The hype around “GTA VI” is deserved—but it conceals a problem. Despite the game’s likely commercial success, developers face shrinking incentives to make anything like it again. A look at the charts suggests that something is wrong in the industry. Since 2020 the five most popular PlayStation games in America each year have come from only eight franchises. The top three have hardly changed at all. “Fortnite” is a relative newcomer at nine years old. The “Call of Duty” franchise is 23. “GTA” is 29, older than many of its players.

It is not only on consoles that gaming culture has ossified. In 2025 only 14% of playing time on PCs was spent on games released that year, according to data from Steam, a games store. In recent years the top ten PC franchises have racked up nearly as much play time as the next 100,000 combined. This concentration at the top represents “the biggest threat to gaming as we’ve known it for 30 to 40 years”, says Mat Piscatella, a former industry executive now at Circana, a market-research firm.

How did gaming get so stuck? Playing “GTA VI” makes clear the formidable barriers faced by new entrants to the industry. The game’s map stretches from the thumping nightclubs of Vice City to alligator-infested swamps, all of it painstakingly populated with a cast of eccentric characters. Leonida has a public transport system and in-game radio stations; Jason even has a console on which you can play games within the game. Every inch is rendered with near-photographic realism.

As technical possibilities have expanded, developing a video game has become a task that makes producing a Hollywood blockbuster look quick and cheap. As games get bigger and graphically richer, making them needs more manpower. The first “Call of Duty” (2003) names 261 people on its closing credits. The latest, released last month, credits 7,060 (more than any “Avengers” film).

Raph Koster, a game-industry veteran, estimates that the cost of developing a top-quality game has risen tenfold every decade since the mid-1990s. “GTA VI” reportedly cost over $1bn—and it shows in every detail, from the swish of Lucia’s ponytail as she flees across rooftops, to the wake of Jason’s speedboat as he chases a seaplane. One developer has compared making the game to building “a pyramid on Everest”. (As budgets have swollen larger than Hollywood’s, apparently so have egos.)

Companies are responding by making fewer, bigger bets. Xbox, Microsoft’s gaming division, has jettisoned some of its smaller studios to focus on reliable performers like “Call of Duty” and “Minecraft”. Rather than gamble on new titles, publishers are turning existing hits into constantly evolving “live service” games, notes Niko Partners, a research firm. Whereas “GTA IV” (2008) was mainly a single-player game, selling 25m copies in five years, “GTA V” (2013) has become an open-ended online experience, selling 230m copies over more than a decade. Despite its age, the franchise made more than $800m last year.

Even for companies with deep pockets, breaking into gaming’s top tier has become tough. In 2024 Sony launched “Concord”, a live-service shooting game with a reported nine-figure budget—only to shut it down after two weeks, amid weak demand. Earlier this month Sony cancelled another shooter, “Fairgames”, after lukewarm feedback. Players have invested so much time and money in titles such as “GTA” and “Fortnite”—honing expertise and buying in-game items—that moving to another game represents a steep cost. The top live-service titles have earned the nickname “black-hole games”, from which players cannot be dragged away.

Some believe that artificial intelligence could shake up the market by allowing developers to generate code, graphics, music and so on more quickly and cheaply. Tim Sweeney, head of Epic Games, which makes “Fortnite”, has said he expects AI to bring forth “a new golden age of gaming”.

Yet even if AI reduces the cost of making software, it is pushing up the price of hardware. Soaring demand from data centres for computer memory has caused a cost surge dubbed the “RAMageddon”. Earlier this year PlayStation and Xbox raised their prices; both consoles now cost more than when they launched six years ago. Analysts believe the next generation of consoles may cost over $1,000. Xbox is laying off thousands of workers. “The future of Xbox itself is now an open question,” argue Gareth Sutcliffe and colleagues at Enders Analysis, a research firm.

All this could mean that the future of gaming looks more like the past. In a world of $1,000 consoles, consumers will shift to lower-spec devices, such as cheap PCs and mobiles, says Mr Piscatella, who notes that games like “Fortnite” and “Minecraft” have been designed to run “on a toaster”. Nintendo has struck gold with its Switch console, which lacks the computing muscle to run games like “GTA VI” but has been a hit thanks to its portability and low price.

Youngsters are gravitating towards Roblox, a free platform featuring millions of basic games made by users. AI is making it easier for tiny development teams to turn out cheap and cheerful experiences for the platform. Roblox recently said that two games in its top 20, “Break and Steal an Egg” and “Huss Valley”, had been created “almost entirely” with AI.

To hardcore gamers, such titles will feel like a step back. Most of the top games on Roblox look like titles from 20 years ago. Nintendo’s latest Switch has the computing power of a console from the 2010s. Yet as the economics of launching new top-tier games get harder, and audiences shift to lower-powered devices, these will be the games that most people play. The decade-long gestation and billion-dollar budget behind “GTA VI” have created a one-of-a-kind piece of entertainment. As one in-game character reflects: “Enjoy this, dude. If this right now was all that there is, all the time—it’d be perfect.” ■

The latest, released last month, credits 7,060 (more than any “Avengers” film).

Raph Koster, a game-industry veteran, estimates that the cost of developing a top-quality game has risen tenfold every decade since the mid-1990s. “GTA VI” reportedly cost over $1bn—and it shows in every detail, from the swish of Lucia’s ponytail as she flees across rooftops, to the wake of Jason’s speedboat as he chases a seaplane. One developer has compared making the game to building “a pyramid on Everest”. (As budgets have swollen larger than Hollywood’s, apparently so have egos.)

Companies are responding by making fewer, bigger bets. Xbox, Microsoft’s gaming division, has jettisoned some of its smaller studios to focus on reliable performers like “Call of Duty” and “Minecraft”. Rather than gamble on new titles, publishers are turning existing hits into constantly evolving “live service” games, notes Niko Partners, a research firm. Whereas “GTA IV” (2008) was mainly a single-player game, selling 25m copies in five years, “GTA V” (2013) has become an open-ended online experience, selling 230m copies over more than a decade. Despite its age, the franchise made more than $800m last year.

Even for companies with deep pockets, breaking into gaming’s top tier has become tough. In 2024 Sony launched “Concord”, a live-service shooting game with a reported nine-figure budget—only to shut it down after two weeks, amid weak demand. Earlier this month Sony cancelled another shooter, “Fairgames”, after lukewarm feedback. Players have invested so much time and money in titles such as “GTA” and “Fortnite”—honing expertise and buying in-game items—that moving to another game represents a steep cost. The top live-service titles have earned the nickname “black-hole games”, from which players cannot be dragged away.

Some believe that artificial intelligence could shake up the market by allowing developers to generate code, graphics, music and so on more quickly and cheaply. Tim Sweeney, head of Epic Games, which makes “Fortnite”, has said he expects AI to bring forth “a new golden age of gaming”.

Yet even if AI reduces the cost of making software, it is pushing up the price of hardware. Soaring demand from data centres for computer memory has caused a cost surge dubbed the “RAMageddon”. Earlier this year PlayStation and Xbox raised their prices; both consoles now cost more than when they launched six years ago. Analysts believe the next generation of consoles may cost over $1,000. Xbox is laying off thousands of workers. “The future of Xbox itself is now an open question,” argue Gareth Sutcliffe and colleagues at Enders Analysis, a research firm.

All this could mean that the future of gaming looks more like the past. In a world of $1,000 consoles, consumers will shift to lower-spec devices, such as cheap PCs and mobiles, says Mr Piscatella, who notes that games like “Fortnite” and “Minecraft” have been designed to run “on a toaster”. Nintendo has struck gold with its Switch console, which lacks the computing muscle to run games like “GTA VI” but has been a hit thanks to its portability and low price.

Youngsters are gravitating towards Roblox, a free platform featuring millions of basic games made by users. AI is making it easier for tiny development teams to turn out cheap and cheerful experiences for the platform. Roblox recently said that two games in its top 20, “Break and Steal an Egg” and “Huss Valley”, had been created “almost entirely” with AI.

To hardcore gamers, such titles will feel like a step back. Most of the top games on Roblox look like titles from 20 years ago. Nintendo’s latest Switch has the computing power of a console from the 2010s. Yet as the economics of launching new top-tier games get harder, and audiences shift to lower-powered devices, these will be the games that most people play. The decade-long gestation and billion-dollar budget behind “GTA VI” have created a one-of-a-kind piece of entertainment. As one in-game character reflects: “Enjoy this, dude. If this right now was all that there is, all the time—it’d be perfect.” ■

articles.title: How Ukraine brought out the EU’s stubborn streak
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
Aesop’s tortoise would have felt at home in Brussels. Slow-moving, deliberative and apparently untroubled by the spectacle of nimbler creatures racing ahead, the plodding reptile shares many qualities with the European Union. The ancient fable has the hare dashing off showily before losing interest in the race. Ukraine’s struggle against Russian revanchism has offered a modern retelling. America originally sprinted ahead as Europe dithered; politicians in Washington were on hand to deliver missiles to Ukraine even as those in Berlin were offering to send helmets.

Yet for all its military prowess America’s enthusiasm has proved erratic, to put it mildly. Europe, by contrast, has spent four years inching forward. Yes, it has squabbled over many decisions and sometimes seemed incapable of getting out of its own way. But in its own unflashy manner the European tortoise has kept moving, powered by a determination seemingly greater than its public disagreements. What it lacks in agility, the EU has made up for in staying power.

The remarkable thing is not how slowly Europe has moved, but that it has kept moving at all. The continent’s endurance in supporting Ukraine has surprised even its supporters. For years suspicions have abounded that “war fatigue” was about to sap the continent’s resolve. (Ukrainians, plenty fatigued, do not alas have the luxury of deciding they have had enough.) And yet look who keeps showing up to help, even as America has at times seemed to put more pressure on Ukraine than Russia. Just this week the process of unlocking a further €45bn ($49bn) in EU financial support to Ukraine has begun, no matter the strained public finances of many member states. The bloc is embarking on a 22nd round of sanctions, undeterred by the fractious haggling that was a feature of the 21 previous rounds. Talks with Ukraine about joining the EU—or at least closely integrating it into the club pending full membership further down the line—are ongoing. Nearly five years into the fighting, millions of Ukrainians enjoy refugee-like protection (and generous welfare provisions) wherever in Europe they might choose to settle. Fatigued, moi?

Granted, EU decision-making about Ukraine sometimes makes tortoises look dynamic. The most recent squabbling has concerned who might represent Europe at peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. For years now the continent has been asked to come up with preferably a single person to represent its interests at the negotiating table. Jared Kushner, the presidential son-in-law who serves as one of America’s envoys, recently quipped that getting Europe to agree on just one interlocutor was harder than getting Russia to accept having them at the negotiating table at all. As if to prove his point, at a summit on November 13th the Europeans put forward a team of no fewer than seven representatives to speak for them—one each from Germany, France, Britain, Italy, Poland, the EU institutions and NATO. (No Luxembourg?) It may seem absurd to have more Europeans at the table than every other party combined. But the truly mad feature of the talks is that America is sitting in the chair of mediator, seemingly neutral between the Ukrainian victim and the Russian aggressor. For its part, Europe is unambiguously on the side of Ukraine.

Unity of purpose is perhaps unsurprising among EU countries fearful that they might be next on President Vladimir Putin’s menu if Ukraine loses (and many of which already face nebulous “hybrid attacks” steered from the Kremlin). Some disagreements have been unedifying. Greece recently wangled an exemption from EU sanctions so its shipping fleet could keep ferrying Russian gas. Belgium has stood in the way of Europe seizing frozen Russian assets that many would like to see handed over to Ukraine. Promising Ukraine will join the EU is laudable, and could one day be a large carrot to get Ukrainians to accept a painful peace involving territorial losses to Russia. Yet in Brussels diplomatic circles the prospect is thought to be at least a decade away. If that might justifiably come as a disappointment to Ukrainians, who once hoped to join by 2027, they could be reminded that America suddenly eased sanctions on Russia ahead of midterm elections earlier this month. Better a plodding friend than a fickle one.

Slow-and-steady as the Europeans have been, there is always a risk that their resolve will reach its limits. Notably, a slew of forthcoming elections could shift the calculus of solidarity. At least three of the five European countries in the negotiating group will go to the polls in 2027. Populists in Italy and Poland are pro-Ukraine, but might need support from Kyiv-bashing allies to form coalitions. The biggest risk is the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidency. Although her tone on Ukraine has softened—and her xenophobic National Rally party is no longer financed by a Russian bank—she says France cannot afford to send more money to the cause. Somewhat in anticipation, European leaders are seeing if they might hurriedly sign off on a long-term EU budget that includes an additional €100bn in funding for Ukraine, locking in support before the political winds change.

Europe’s plodding yet purposeful approach has worked well enough so long as the job has been merely to keep Ukraine supplied with money, weapons and prospects for the future. Peace negotiations may demand something different. Alas, for now substantive talks seem a distant prospect. Russia continues to issue impossible demands as a precondition for bringing its war of aggression to an end, including NATO troops being pulled out of central Europe. Mr Putin seems to be betting that another winter of fighting will wear down Ukrainian resistance. Should a deal come within reach, Europe may need to move faster than it is used to. Until then, the tortoise has little reason to envy the hare.■

articles.title: The next stop for Europe’s failed asylum-seekers: Rwanda
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
“A TRULY HISTORIC paradigm shift”. “A game-changer”. “One big milestone”. If officials are cautious about overselling Europe’s asylum deal with Rwanda, no one told the politicians from five European governments who unveiled it in Vienna on November 16th. “This is the first real answer anyone has put on the table to solve the deep problems with the current system,” said Mette Frederiksen, Denmark’s prime minister.

Under the plan, which is promised to take effect next year, migrants in the five countries—Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands—whose asylum bids have been rejected may be transferred to a “return hub” in Rwanda. They will be able to integrate into local communities, return home or move to another country ready to accept them, said Vincent Biruta, Rwanda’s interior minister, speaking with European ministers whom his government had assiduously courted. Officials say Rwanda will now sign bilateral agreements with all five governments.

The Rwanda plan is a new element of Europe’s migration “turnaround”. Thanks partly to calmer conditions near its borders, irregular arrivals have plummeted (see chart 1). Last month saw the fewest asylum claims in Germany since October 2011. An “asylum pact” that took effect in June helps. But it is hard to deport asylum-seekers whose bids have failed. Lacking documentation, or coming from countries that do not co-operate, many fall into the shadows. The EU issues far more return orders than it carries out (see chart 2 ).

Politicians want to show they can do things previously seen as impossible, says Raphael Bossong from the German Institute for International and Security Affairs in Berlin. But where populist-right ones demand “remigration”, the mainstream seeks a more orderly approach. In October the EU passed a law allowing the creation of return hubs, with human-rights and monitoring safeguards. That, say officials, puts the scheme on a sounder legal footing than other efforts. Britain’s ill-fated 2022 deal, which unlike the European scheme would have sent migrants to Rwanda to process their asylum claims, cost taxpayers £715m ($910m) before being abandoned.

Details are scant and questions remain. The first is effectiveness. The few hundred migrants at most who could be sent to Rwanda next year will not make a dent in the stock of failed asylum-seekers in Europe. Germany alone has over 250,000 migrants served with return orders. The “bigger number”, Ms Frederiksen said, would be migrants who, hearing of the Rwanda scheme, might decide not to travel to Europe. But would minds really be changed by the remote possibility of being sent to Rwanda? “Evidence of a deterrent effect is highly uncertain,” said a British official of his country’s scheme, which had a more credible claim to deterrence since it would have applied to more migrants.

Second, what would actually happen to those sent to Rwanda, one of Africa’s poorer and most densely populated countries? Human-rights groups fear, once migrants are beyond Europe’s gaze, they could face mistreatment or further deportation, including refoulement into danger. “This is a hugely repressive regime,” says Tineke Strik, a Dutch Green member of the European Parliament. But such concerns rarely trouble European officials attacked by critics they see as naive do-gooders. “Unless you put a hub in Liechtenstein you’ll run out of options,” sniffs one. The new deal has a role for United Nations migration and refugee agencies in offering advice, monitoring conditions and aiding integration. Rwanda already hosts EU-funded centres for refugees who have been evacuated from Libya. Even so, legal challenges to the new plan are certain.

Others worry what the deal may mean for relations with Rwanda, which has supported a murderous militia in the Democratic Republic of Congo and persecutes dissidents (one was recently found beheaded in Uganda). “It is deeply troubling that European governments are considering sending rejected asylum-seekers to Rwanda,” says Rémy Amahirwa, a Sweden-based Rwandan whose mother, an opposition figure, has been imprisoned by Paul Kagame’s government. Last year the German government cancelled talks with Rwanda because of its actions in Congo. Europeans want to distinguish Rwanda’s treatment of migrants from its broader human-rights record. Yet some envoys say they already detect signs of diplomatic reticence from European governments.

Beyond diplomatic cover, what is in it for Mr Kagame? Mr Biruta said Rwanda was just doing its bit to manage the problem of irregular immigration. In reality it hopes for cash, aid projects and a reputation as a reliable partner. It also wants to select who comes, with a preference for professionals who can integrate into labour markets and boost the local economy. “They feel bruised from the UK arrangements, so there is a real interest to make this work,” says one European official.

Not everyone in Europe is on board. In Germany doubts among Social Democrats, the junior ruling coalition partner, extend into the cabinet. France and Spain, among others, remain sceptical. Yet both countries may elect right-wing governments during the next six months. Europe’s rightward march on migration policy is likely to continue.

Other EU countries, notably Italy, are clamouring to join the return-hub plan—even Britain may be interested—and European governments are reportedly negotiating with other potential return-hub hosts. Meanwhile, plans are being drawn up to avoid a repeat of the scenes earlier this year, when tens of thousands of Moroccans swarmed into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Frontex, Europe’s border-guard agency, may have its mandate expanded; it may also help with deportations to Rwanda. Ultimately some governments aspire to externalise the entire asylum process. One official says it is vital for centrist politicians to take action now to see off something nastier from right-wing populists: “It’s important we get this right, otherwise we’ll be in deep shit in a few years.”■
